sources.news_title: US delegation's departure for Iran talks in Pakistan delayed for 'policy meetings': Reports
sources.text:
Rabia Iclal Turan
21 April 2026•Update: 21 April 2026
A US delegation’s planned departure for Pakistan for a second round of face-to-face talks with Iran was delayed Tuesday due to “additional policy meetings” in Washington, according to US media reports.
Vice President JD Vance, who is expected to travel to Islamabad, remained in Washington to attend the meetings at the White House, said a US official, according to The New York Times.
A White House official said as of Tuesday afternoon, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance were still meeting with President Donald Trump and his advisers.
The departure was postponed for “additional policy meetings” involving Vance, without specifying a new timeline, according to a White House official cited by The Washington Post.
The delay comes as uncertainty surrounds the next round of negotiations between Washington and Tehran, with Iran yet to confirm its participation in the talks, and demanding the lifting of a US blockade in the Strait of Hormuz as a precondition.
The two sides held a first round of high-level, face-to-face engagement in Pakistan earlier this month, but those talks ended without a deal.

sources.news_title: U.S. puts negotiations with Iran on hold as ceasefire deadline nears
sources.text:
Trump says U.S. will extend its ceasefire with Iran at Pakistan’s request
In a Truth Social post announcing the ceasefire extension, the president also said the U.S. military would continue it’s blockade of Iranian ports.
ISLAMABAD, Pakistan — President Donald Trump said Tuesday the United States is extending its ceasefire with Iran at Pakistan’s request as he waits for a unified proposal from the Islamic Republic.
The announcement came as last-minute ceasefire talks between the U.S. and Iran looked uncertain and a two-week truce was set to expire Wednesday.
Earlier, the White House put on hold Vice President JD Vance’s expected trip to Islamabad for a second round of talks as Tehran — at least for the time being — has balked at further talks.
In a Truth Social post announcing the ceasefire extension, Trump also said the U.S. military would continue it’s blockade of Iranian ports.
As last-minute ceasefire talks between the U.S. and Iran looked uncertain, both countries warned that, without a deal, they were prepared to resume fighting.
Pakistani leaders, including Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, worked intensively late Tuesday to get both sides to agree to a second round of ceasefire talks, according to two officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei told Iran’s state TV there has been “no final decision” on whether to attend because of “unacceptable actions” by the U.S., apparently referencing its recent blockade in the Strait of Hormuz.
As Vance put on hold a return trip to Islamabad, Pakistan’s capital, Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were expected in Washington on Tuesday afternoon for consultations about how to proceed, said a U.S. official who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal administration deliberations.
The official cautioned that Trump could change his mind on negotiating with Iran at any time, and declined to predict what would happen if the current ceasefire expires without another meeting. The official said Trump has options short of restarting airstrikes.
Both sides remain dug in rhetorically
Before announcing the ceasefire extension, Trump had warned that “lots of bombs” will “start going off” if there’s no agreement before the Wednesday deadline, while Iran’s chief negotiator said that Tehran has “new cards on the battlefield” that haven’t yet been revealed.
A senior commander in Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps threatened to destroy the region’s oil industry if war with the United States resumes. “If southern neighbors allow the enemy to use their facilities to attack Iran, they should say goodbye to oil production in the Middle East region,” Gen. Majid Mousavi told an Iranian news site.
Strait of Hormuz control key to negotiations
Iran’s envoy to the United Nations said Tuesday that Tehran has “received some sign” that the U.S. is ready to stop its blockade of Iranian ports. The U.S. had made no public statements about lifting the blockade.
Ambassador Amir Saeid Iravani said ending the blockade remains a condition for Iran to rejoin peace talks. When that happens, he said, “I think the next round of the negotiations will take place.”
The U.S. imposed the blockade to pressure Tehran into ending its stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping lane through which 20% of the world’s natural gas and crude oil transits in peacetime.
Iran’s grip on the strait has sent oil prices soaring. Brent crude, the international standard, was trading at close to $95 per barrel on Tuesday, up more than 30% from Feb. 28, the day that Israel and the U.S. attacked Iran to start the war.
Before the war began, the Strait of Hormuz had been fully open to international shipping. Trump has demanded that vessels again be allowed to transit unimpeded.
Over the weekend, Iran said that it had received new proposals from Washington, but also suggested that a wide gap remains between the sides. Issues that derailed the last round of negotiations included Iran’s nuclear enrichment program, its regional proxies and the strait.
U.S. says its forces board sanctioned oil tanker
On Tuesday, the U.S. said its forces boarded an oil tanker previously sanctioned for smuggling Iranian crude oil in Asia. The Pentagon said in a social media post that U.S. forces boarded the M/T Tifani “without incident.”
The U.S. military did not say where the vessel had been boarded, though ship-tracking data showed the Tifani in the Indian Ocean between Sri Lanka and Indonesia on Tuesday. The Pentagon statement added that “international waters are not a refuge for sanctioned vessels.”
The U.S. military on Sunday seized an Iranian container ship, the first interception under the blockade. Iran’s joint military command called the armed boarding an act of piracy and a violation of the ceasefire.
Pakistan hopeful talks will proceed
Pakistani officials have expressed confidence that Iran will also send a delegation to resume talks that mark the highest-level negotiations between the U.S. and Iran since the 1979 Islamic Revolution. The first round April 11 and 12 ended without an agreement.
Pakistan said Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar met Tuesday with the acting U.S. ambassador in Islamabad to urge a ceasefire extension. Dar also met with the ambassador from China, a key trading partner with Iran.
Security has been tightened across Pakistan’s capital, where authorities have deployed thousands of personnel and increased patrols along routes leading to the airport.
Israel jails soldiers for defacing Jesus statue in Lebanon
Israel’s military said Tuesday it has sentenced two soldiers to 30 days in jail and removed them from combat duty for smashing a statue of Jesus Christ in Lebanon. Images of an Israeli soldier with a sledgehammer smashing the statue’s head emerged over the weekend, bringing widespread condemnation.
Israel said one of the soldiers being punished hammered the statue to the ground. The other filmed the destruction. The Israeli military said it replaced the statue.
Meanwhile, historic diplomatic talks between Israel and Lebanon were set to resume on Thursday in Washington, an Israeli, a Lebanese and a U.S. official said. All three spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the behind-the-scenes negotiations.
The Israeli and Lebanese ambassadors met last week for the first direct diplomatic talks in decades. Israel says the talks are aimed at disarming Hezbollah and reaching a peace agreement with Lebanon.
A 10-day ceasefire began on Friday in Lebanon, where fighting between Israel and Iranian-backed Hezbollah militants broke out two days after the U.S. and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran to start the war. Fighting in Lebanon has killed more than 2,290 people.
Since the war started, at least 3,375 people have been killed in Iran, according to authorities. Additionally, 23 people have died in Israel, and more than a dozen in Gulf Arab states. Fifteen Israeli soldiers in Lebanon and 13 U.S. service members throughout the region have been killed.

sources.news_title: Vance’s departure to Pakistan for Iran peace talks delayed: reports
sources.text:
Washington, Apr 21 (PTI) US Vice President JD Vance’s visit to Islamabad, for peace talks with Iran to end the seven-week war, has been put on hold after Tehran failed to respond to American negotiating positions, the New York Times reported on Tuesday.
Vance was scheduled to depart Tuesday morning for Islamabad, where talks were set to resume on Wednesday — the same day the fragile cease-fire between the United States and Iran is set to expire. Without an Iranian response, the diplomatic process is in effect paused, though the trip has not been cancelled, a US official was quoted in the New York Times report.
The trip could be back on at a moment’s notice if Iran’s negotiators respond in a way that President Donald Trump deems acceptable. US officials are also looking for a clear signal that Iran’s negotiators have been fully empowered to reach an agreement, the report said.
The Washington Post attributed the delay to “additional policy meetings” involving Vance at the White House.
Trump accused Iran of violating the ceasefire “numerous times” in a post on Truth Social early Tuesday. In a separate interview with CNBC, he said the United States is “going to end up with a great deal” from the negotiations. “I think they have no choice. We’ve taken out their navy, we’ve taken out their air force, we’ve taken out their leaders,” Trump said.
When asked whether the US would resume bombing if a deal is not reached by Wednesday, Trump said that he expects to “be bombing, because that is a better attitude to go in with.” He added that the military is “raring to go.” PTI SKU RD RD

sources.news_title: JD Vance cancels Pakistan trip as US-Iran talks still uncertain
sources.text:
live
Iran war live updates: Trump extends ceasefire with Iran until 'discussions concluded', JD Vance cancels Pakistan trip
US President Donald Trump has announced on Truth Social he is extending the ceasefire with Iran.
He says he will continue the blockade and extend the ceasefire until discussions are concluded one way or the other.
Vice President, JD Vance, had been due to travel to Pakistan today for a second round of peace talks, but he is yet to leave Washington.
Iran had not confirmed it would participate.
Follow the latest updates with our live blog.
Key Events
Submit a comment or question
Live updates
A recap of the latest developments
- US President Donald Trump has extended the ceasefire until Iran submits a peace proposal.
- The IRGC has threatened to target Gulf countries' oil production if attacks are launched from their territory.
- US Vice-President JD Vance has cancelled his trip to Pakistan where he was to be part of the American delegation in peace talks.
- Iran has still not committed to attending a second round of talks in Islamabad and has called the US blockade an "act of war".
- The EU will bolster its naval mission to the Middle East.
- French President Emmanuel Macron has hosted the Lebanese PM to discuss supporting Lebanon in its negotiations with Israel.
Stay with us as we bring you the latest from the Middle East.
New: Filters
Choose what information you see below by using filters
Pakistan's PM thanks Trump for extending ceasefire
Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has thanked US President Donald Trump for "graciously accepting our request to extend the ceasefire to allow ongoing diplomatic efforts to take their course".
"With the trust and confidence reposed in, Pakistan shall continue its earnest efforts for negotiated settlement of conflict," Sharif said.
He said he hopes both sides continue to observe the ceasefire and could conclude a "comprehensive peace deal" at the next round of talks.
We reported earlier an aide of Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's speaker of the parliament and a top negotiator, called Trump's ceasefire a "ploy to buy time".
Trump's ceasefire extension a 'ploy to buy time', adviser to Iran's top negotiator says
An adviser to Iran’s parliament speaker says US President Donald Trump's ceasefire extension is a "ploy to buy time" for a surprise strike.
Mohammad Qalibaf's adviser said in a post on X that the continuation of the US blockade on Iranian ports was "no different from bombardment and must be met with a military response".
US defence companies report strong earnings and surge in demand
US defence companies are reporting a surge in demand for military equipment, as the war in the Middle East prompts fresh orders from governments around the world.
Defence companies RTX, Northrop Grumman and GE Aerospace all reported increased orders in the first quarter, and GE Aerospace also had a "strong" first quarter, as wars raged in Ukraine and the Middle East.
Growth has been buoyed by announcements from the US aiming to ramp up production of the Tomahawk, Patriot and GEM-T missiles, among other weapons systems.
We previously reported these weapons were seriously depleted when the US burned through almost 12,000 munitions at a cost of $US26 billion ($36.3 billion) in the first 16 days of the conflict.
US undersecretary of defence Jules Hurst said Donald Trump's fiscal 2027 budget requested $US1.5 trillion, describing the demand as a "generational investment in the United States military, the arsenal of freedom".
"This 42 per cent increase will supercharge our defence industrial base by expanding production of major weapon systems while strengthening supply chains and supporting tens of thousands of small- and medium-sized businesses," Hurst said.
Reporting with AFP
📷: Daily life in Tehran during the ceasefire, in pictures
Two IDF soldiers detained over toppling, striking of Jesus statue in Lebanon
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has announced on X it has detained two soldiers responsible for toppling and striking the head of a Jesus statue in southern Lebanon.
The IDF said one soldier damaged the statue, another photographed and six others were present and "did not act to stop the incident or report it".
"The IDF expresses deep regret over the incident and emphasizes that its operations in Lebanon are directed solely against the Hezbollah terrorist organization and other terrorist groups, and not against Lebanese civilians," it said.
Both soldiers will be removed from combat duty and receive 30 days of military detention, according to the IDF.
A photo of a new statue was then shared to the IDF X page with a post saying IDF troops replaced the statue "in full coordination with the local community of Debel".
Lebanon needs more than $800m to 'tackle humanitarian crisis'
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam says the country needs 500 million euros, or about $A820m, to address the war's humanitarian fallout as a fragile 10-day ceasefire holds, despite claims from Israel and the Iran-backed group Hezbollah that both sides have violated the ceasefire.
We reported earlier Salam was meeting French President Emmanuel Macron to discuss French support with negotiations.
"Lebanon needs 500 million euros to tackle the humanitarian crisis over the next six months," Salam said during a joint press conference with Macron.
The death toll in Lebanon is more than 2,400, with thousands more injured, according to Lebanese government agencies.
Macron urged Israel to "renounce its territorial ambitions" in Lebanon, adding that Hezbollah must "cease" firing into Israeli territory and be disarmed "by the Lebanese themselves".
He further called for an agreement between Israel and Lebanon that guarantees "the security of both countries, Lebanon's territorial integrity, and lays the groundwork for the normalisation of their relations".
Reporting with AFP
Key Event
Trump extends ceasefire until 'discussions are concluded'
US President Donald Trump has announced on Truth Social he is extending the ceasefire with Iran.
Trump said due to the "fractured" government of Iran, Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Field Marshal Asim Munir, asked him to "hold" attacks on Iran until "their leaders and representatives can come up with a unified proposal".
"I have therefore directed our military to continue the blockade and, in all other respects, remain ready and able, and will therefore extend the ceasefire until such time as their proposal is submitted, and discussions are concluded, one way or the other," Trump said.
The ceasefire was expected to end tomorrow morning AEST and earlier we reported JD Vance cancelled his trip to Pakistan for peace talks.
Key Event
IRGC threatens Gulf countries' oil production
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has threatened to end oil production in the Middle East if Iran faces attacks launched from its Gulf neighbours' territory, according to a report by AFP, citing state media.
The semi-official Fars news agency quoted threats by Majid Mousavi, commander of the IRGC's aerospace force.
"The southern neighbours should know that if their geography and facilities are used in the service of the enemies to attack the Iranian nation, they should bid farewell to oil production in the Middle East," he said.
In the early stages of the war, oil facilities in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Oman were targeted, helping lead to the sharpest increase in fuel prices since war started in Ukraine.
Lebanon warns Israel to withdraw or face resistance
Lebanon’s parliament speaker has warned Israel to withdraw from the country's south or face resistance, signalling a risk of renewed confrontation.
A 10-day ceasefire between Israel and Lebanon came into effect on Thursday, local time, but Israeli forces have remained on Lebanese land along the entire border.
Israel claims it's creating a buffer zone to shield northern Israel from attacks by militant group Hezbollah.
Ambassadors from Israel and Lebanon are due to meet for further US-mediated talks tomorrow.
Lebanon's parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, who is a Hezbollah ally, said Lebanon could not tolerate losing a metre of land.
If Israel "maintains its occupation, whether of areas, positions, or by drawing yellow lines, it will smell the scent of resistance every day," he said in Lebanese newspaper al-Joumhouria.
Israel has been carrying out demolitions in Lebanon's southern villages since the ceasefire, saying it is acting against infrastructure embedded by Hezbollah in civilian areas.
Reporting with Reuters
US 'creating new obstacles' to talks, senior Iranian official says
Iran could attend talks with the US in Pakistan if Washington abandons its policy of pressure and threats, Reuters reports, citing a senior Iranian official.
The official is quoted saying Tehran rejects negotiations aimed at surrender.
They added Pakistan was continuing efforts to persuade the US to lift its naval blockade and release Iranian-flagged container ship Touska, which was boarded and seized by the US military earlier this week.
He accused Washington of "creating new obstacles every day instead of resolving the differences" to end the war.
Reporting with Reuters
Hezbollah claims responsibility for attack on Israel
Hezbollah claimed responsibility for an attack on northern Israel in retaliation for what it said were Israeli violations of a 10-day ceasefire, the first such claim since the truce began.
AFP reported Hezbollah said in a statement that "in defence of Lebanon and its people, and in response to the blatant" Israeli ceasefire violations including "attacks on civilians and the destruction of their homes and villages", its fighters launched rockets and attack drones at a military site in northern Israel that it said was the source of artillery shelling towards a south Lebanon town.
The Israel Defense Forces announced on X that Hezbollah launched "several" rockets toward IDF soldiers operating in southern Lebanon.
"In response, the IDF struck the launcher from which the rockets were launched," it said.
It also said Israeli forces intercepted a UAV launched from Lebanon.
"The launches constitute a blatant violation of the ceasefire agreement," it said.
The IDF has claimed a number of ceasefire violations from Hezbollah in recent days, announcing on X that they eliminated "armed terrorists" who approached IDF troops in southern Lebanon.
Key Event
Vance calls off trip to Pakistan as ceasefire expiry draws closer
US Vice-President JD Vance has called off his trip to Pakistan, according to AP, citing a US official.
Confusion has lingered for days after it emerged Mr Vance was supposed to lead the US delegation to peace talks in Islamabad, but it was unclear whether they would meet any Iranian delegation.
Pakistani leaders, including Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, worked intensively late Tuesday to get both sides to agree to a second round of ceasefire talks, according to AP, citing two officials who spoke on condition of anonymity.
The ceasefire is set to end this morning, Australian time.
EU bolsters naval mission in Middle East
The European Union has agreed to increase sanctions against Iran to include those responsible for blocking the Strait of Hormuz.
The decision was made after a meeting of foreign ministers in Luxembourg overnight.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she had asked countries to bolster the naval mission in the Middle East currently protecting ships from attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebel group in the Red Sea.
France hosts Lebanese PM
Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and French President Emmanuel Macron have met in Paris to discuss how to help Lebanon with negotiations with Israel later this week.
The US will host the ambassador-level talks between Israel and Lebanon on Thursday, although it remains unclear whether the objective is to extend a fragile 10-day ceasefire between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah or pave the way for deeper negotiations.
Israel accuses Hezbollah of 'blatant' ceasefire violation
Israel says the Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah has fired several rockets toward its troops operating in southern Lebanon in what it's described as a "blatant violation" of the ceasefire agreement.
The 10-day ceasefire enters its second half with ambassadors from Israel and Lebanon due to meet for talks in Washington tomorrow.
But Israel's continued presence in south Lebanon is causing tension in the fragile ceasefire.
Sirens sounded in northern Israeli communities overnight but they were likely triggered by the interception of a drone launched from Lebanon before it crossed into Israeli territory.
Iran's foreign minister calls US blockade 'act of war'
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said the US blockade of Iranian ports was an "act of war" and thus a violation of the ceasefire.
"Iran knows how to neutralize restrictions, how to defend its interests, and how to resist bullying," he said in a post on X .
Shipping through Strait of Hormuz still at a standstill
The Strait of Hormuz is still effectively closed to ships — just three vessels have made it through the vital shipping route in the past 24 hours.
Shipping data shows two vessels with no known flag or country of ownership sailing through the strait overnight after calling in at an Iranian port.
The Meda liquefied petroleum gas tanker, which had called in at an United Arab Emirates port, transited the strait on Monday, local time.
Hundreds of ships and 20,000 seafarers are still stuck inside the Gulf.
Key Event
JD Vance still in Washington, official says
US Vice-President JD Vance, expected to lead a US delegation at upcoming negotiations with Iran in Pakistan, was still in Washington at Tuesday lunchtime, local time, to participate in meetings, the White House has said.
"Additional policy meetings are taking place at the White House in which the vice president will participate," an official said in a brief statement sent to AFP.
The official did not provide further details. But Vance's departure, which has been the subject of contradictory announcements, was scheduled for Tuesday morning, according to recent reports.
Meanwhile, Axios and the New York Times are reporting that Vance's trip to Pakistan has been put on hold.
Reporting with AFP
Iran executes accused over January protest
Overnight, Iranian authorities executed a man they say was convicted of helping to set fire to a major mosque in Tehran during protests in January.

Trump says the US will extend its ceasefire with Iran at Pakistan’s request
ISLAMABAD (AP) — President Donald Trump said Tuesday the United States is extending its ceasefire with Iran at Pakistan’s request as he waits for a unified proposal from the Islamic Republic.
The announcement came as last-minute ceasefire talks between the U.S. and Iran looked uncertain and a two-week truce was set to expire Wednesday.
Earlier, the White House put on hold Vice President JD Vance’s expected trip to Islamabad for a second round of talks as Tehran — at least for the time-being — has balked at further talks.
In a Truth Social post announcing the ceasefire extension, Trump said the U.S. military would “remain ready and able, and will therefore extend the Ceasefire until such time as their proposal is submitted, and discussions are concluded, one way or the other.” He said the U.S. would continue it’s blockade of Iranian ports.
Both countries have warned that, without a deal, they were prepared to resume fighting.
Pakistan scrambles to get US and Iran to negotiate
Pakistani leaders, including Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, worked intensively late Tuesday to get both sides to agree to a second round of ceasefire talks, according to two officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei told Iran’s state TV there has been “no final decision” on whether to agree to more talks because of “unacceptable actions” by the U.S., apparently referencing its recent blockade in the Strait of Hormuz.
As Vance put on hold a return trip to Islamabad, Pakistan’s capital, Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were expected in Washington on Tuesday afternoon for consultations about how to proceed, said a U.S. official who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal administration deliberations.
The official cautioned that Trump could change his mind on negotiating with Iran at any time, and declined to predict what would happen if the ceasefire expires without another meeting. The official said Trump has options short of restarting airstrikes.
Both sides remain dug in rhetorically
Before announcing the ceasefire extension, Trump had warned that “lots of bombs” will “start going off” if there’s no agreement before the Wednesday deadline, while Iran’s chief negotiator said that Tehran has “new cards on the battlefield” that haven’t yet been revealed.
A senior commander in Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps threatened to destroy the region’s oil industry if war with the United States resumes. “If southern neighbors allow the enemy to use their facilities to attack Iran, they should say goodbye to oil production in the Middle East region,” Gen. Majid Mousavi told an Iranian news site.
Strait of Hormuz control key to negotiations
Iran’s envoy to the United Nations said Tuesday that Tehran has “received some sign” that the U.S. is ready to stop its blockade of Iranian ports. The U.S. had made no public statements about lifting the blockade.
Ambassador Amir Saeid Iravani said ending the blockade remains a condition for Iran to rejoin peace talks. When that happens, he said, “I think the next round of the negotiations will take place.”
The U.S. imposed the blockade to pressure Tehran into ending its stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping lane through which 20% of the world’s natural gas and crude oil transits in peacetime.
Iran’s grip on the strait has sent oil prices soaring. Brent crude, the international standard, was trading at close to $95 per barrel on Tuesday, up more than 30% from Feb. 28, the day that Israel and the U.S. attacked Iran to start the war.
Before the war began, the Strait of Hormuz had been fully open to international shipping. Trump has demanded that vessels again be allowed to transit unimpeded.
Over the weekend, Iran said that it had received new proposals from Washington, but also suggested that a wide gap remains between the sides. Issues that derailed the last round of negotiations included Iran’s nuclear enrichment program, its regional proxies and the strait.
US says its forces board sanctioned oil tanker
On Tuesday, the U.S. said its forces boarded an oil tanker previously sanctioned for smuggling Iranian crude oil in Asia. The Pentagon said in a social media post that U.S. forces boarded the M/T Tifani “without incident.”
The U.S. military did not say where the vessel had been boarded, though ship-tracking data showed the Tifani in the Indian Ocean between Sri Lanka and Indonesia on Tuesday. The Pentagon statement added that “international waters are not a refuge for sanctioned vessels.”
The U.S. military on Sunday seized an Iranian container ship, the first interception under the blockade. Iran’s joint military command called the armed boarding an act of piracy and a violation of the ceasefire.
Pakistan hopeful talks will proceed
Pakistani officials have expressed confidence that Iran will also send a delegation to resume talks that mark the highest-level negotiations between the U.S. and Iran since the 1979 Islamic Revolution. The first round April 11 and 12 ended without an agreement.
Pakistan said Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar met Tuesday with the acting U.S. ambassador in Islamabad to urge a ceasefire extension. Dar also met with the ambassador from China, a key trading partner with Iran.
Security has been tightened across Pakistan’s capital, where authorities have deployed thousands of personnel and increased patrols along routes leading to the airport.
Talks between Israel and Lebanon set to resume
In Lebanon, the Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah said in a statement it had fired rockets and drones at Israeli forces for the first time since a 10-day truce took effect Friday “in response to the blatant and documented violations” by Israel, which it said included “attacks on civilians and the destruction of their homes and villages in southern Lebanon.”
The Israeli army said it responded by striking the group’s rocket launcher. Israeli officials have said they intend to maintain a buffer zone in southern Lebanon — an area that includes dozens of villages whose residents have not been allowed to return.
Historic diplomatic talks between Israel and Lebanon are set to resume on Thursday in Washington, an Israeli, a Lebanese and a U.S. official said. All three spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the behind-the-scenes negotiations.
The Israeli and Lebanese ambassadors met last week for the first direct diplomatic talks in decades. Israel says the talks are aimed at disarming Hezbollah and reaching a peace agreement with Lebanon.
A 10-day ceasefire began on Friday in Lebanon, where fighting between Israel and Iranian-backed Hezbollah militants broke out two days after the U.S. and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran to start the war. Fighting in Lebanon has killed more than 2,290 people.
Since the war started, at least 3,375 people have been killed in Iran, according to authorities. Additionally, 23 people have died in Israel and more than a dozen in Gulf Arab states. Fifteen Israeli soldiers in Lebanon and 13 U.S. service members throughout the region have been killed.

sources.news_title: Vance Embarrassed as Trump's Peace Talks Slip Into Chaos
sources.text:
A fresh diplomatic setback has put the spotlight on JD Vance, as efforts led by Donald Trump to broker peace with Iran descended into confusion and uncertainty.
Vance was expected to travel to Pakistan to lead a crucial round of peace talks aimed at extending a fragile ceasefire in the ongoing conflict. However, the trip was abruptly thrown into doubt after Iran failed to confirm its participation, leaving the US delegation in limbo.
The situation quickly turned awkward, with Vance reportedly on standby while plans kept shifting. The delay not only disrupted the diplomatic schedule but also raised questions about coordination within the US administration.
Adding to the confusion were Trump’s conflicting statements. At different points, he suggested Vance might not travel due to security concerns, only to later claim that the vice president was already on his way — even as reports indicated he remained in Washington.
Meanwhile, tensions with Iran continued to escalate. Tehran reportedly backed out of the talks unless certain conditions, including easing of US pressure measures, were met. With both sides holding firm, the peace effort struggled to gain traction.
The uncertainty has also cast a shadow over the ceasefire itself, which is nearing its deadline. Trump has signaled little interest in extending it, even as global observers warn of renewed conflict if negotiations fail.
The episode highlights the growing challenges in US diplomatic strategy, where aggressive posturing and mixed messaging appear to be undermining negotiations.
For Vance, the stalled trip has turned into an uncomfortable moment, exposing the fragility of the administration’s peace push.
As the situation unfolds, the chances of a breakthrough remain unclear, with the peace process now hanging in the balance.

sources.news_title: Vance's departure to Islamabad put on hold as Iran fails to respond
sources.text:
US-Iran peace talks in Islamabad face delay as Tehran fails to respond to American negotiating positions, raising concerns about the fragile ceasefire.
Key Points
- US-Iran peace talks in Islamabad are delayed due to Tehran's lack of response to US negotiating positions.
- The planned visit of US Vice President JD Vance to Islamabad has been put on hold.
- President Trump accuses Iran of violating the ceasefire and suggests a potential resumption of bombing if no deal is reached.
- US officials seek assurance that Iranian negotiators are fully empowered to reach an agreement.
United States Vice President J D Vance's visit to Islamabad, for peace talks with Iran to end the seven-week war, has been put on hold after Tehran failed to respond to American negotiating positions, the New York Times reported on Tuesday.
Vance's Planned Trip and Ceasefire Expiry
Vance was scheduled to depart Tuesday morning for Islamabad, where talks were set to resume on Wednesday -- the same day the fragile cease-fire between the United States and Iran is set to expire.
Without an Iranian response, the diplomatic process is in effect paused, though the trip has not been cancelled, a US official was quoted in the New York Times report.
Conditions for Resuming Talks
The trip could be back on at a moment's notice if Iran's negotiators respond in a way that President Donald Trump deems acceptable. US officials are also looking for a clear signal that Iran's negotiators have been fully empowered to reach an agreement, the report said.
The Washington Post attributed the delay to 'additional policy meetings' involving Vance at the White House.
Trump's Accusations and Stance
Trump accused Iran of violating the ceasefire 'numerous times' in a post on Truth Social early Tuesday.
In a separate interview with CNBC, he said the United States is 'going to end up with a great deal' from the negotiations.
"I think they have no choice. We've taken out their navy, we've taken out their air force, we've taken out their leaders," Trump said.
Potential Resumption of Bombing
When asked whether the US would resume bombing if a deal is not reached by Wednesday, Trump said that he expects to 'be bombing, because that is a better attitude to go in with'.
He added that the military is 'raring to go'.
The US and Iran do not have formal diplomatic relations; the Swiss government represents US interests in Iran.
The US has a long history of imposing sanctions on Iran over its nuclear programme and support for militant groups.
These sanctions have significantly impacted Iran's economy.
